video_title: Ørsted CEO: Offshore Wind's Boom and Bust, and America's Pushback | Podcast | In Good Company
gist: Ørsted CEO Rasmus Errboe details the offshore wind boom-and-bust: a 70% cost decline from 2015-2020 reversed by roughly 50% from 2020-2025, a US stop-work order on an 80%-complete project that triggered a lawsuit against the US government, and an 8 billion euro capital raise. He argues geopolitics and affordability, not just climate, now drive a European renewables buildout as electricity demand heads toward doubling by 2050.

themes.theme: US Political Risk and the Stop-Work Order

insights.claim: The US government issued a stop-work order on an Ørsted offshore wind project that was 80% complete, effectively converting a near-finished asset into a liability with no cash flow.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Late-stage regulatory reversal risk in the US is now a live, materialized threat for renewables developers, not a tail scenario; underwrite US projects with abandonment optionality in mind.
insights.quote: building the bridge and then being asked to stop your construction 50 m before uh the you you build the paying terminal. You have it all built but you don't get your cash flow.

insights.claim: Ørsted sued the US government on September 4 2025 over the stop-work order, resting its case on seven-to-nine years of secured permits.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Litigation against a sovereign signals the developer sees strong legal merits; watch the case outcome as a precedent for permit sanctity and potential recovery of stranded US capital.
insights.quote: we looked at the merits and we looked at the facts and we looked at the permits. We we had spent seven seven to nine years to get the permits in place.

insights.claim: The stop-work order landed mid-way through Ørsted's 8 billion euro equity raise, forcing management to protect the capital raise over a single weekend while shutting down the project.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Illustrates how concentrated event risk can strike at the worst possible funding moment; a signal of the fragility premium embedded in renewables equity stories.

insights.claim: Ørsted's self-critical lesson is that it should have stepped back from troubled US projects sooner, having set targets too high and over-indexed on volume rather than value at its June 2023 capital markets day.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Management admitting a volume-over-value error signals a strategic pivot toward disciplined capital allocation; a marker for whether future guidance is more conservative.
insights.quote: we set the bar too high on the capital markets day we were too focused on on volume rather than value um and then we didn't step step step away fast enough

themes.theme: Offshore Wind Cost Cycle and Economics

insights.claim: The levelized cost of electricity for offshore wind fell roughly 70% from 2015 to 2020, then rose roughly 50% from 2020 to 2025, driven by rising interest rates, supply chain cost inflation, and unhealthy competition from oil and gas entrants.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the boom-bust magnitude; the cost reversal explains the sector's failed tenders and writedowns and frames the entry point for the next cost-out cycle.
insights.quote: LCE to go down by roughly 70% from 15 to 20. From 20 to 25, we have seen LCE going up again with roughly 50, so 50%.

insights.claim: Offshore wind economics are now stabilizing after the 2020-2025 reset, with Ørsted's CEO expecting a renewed cost-out (cost decline) ahead.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: A CEO call that the sector has passed its cost trough; a bullish inflection signal for developers and suppliers if realized.
insights.quote: Now it seems as if we are sort of on the other side and we are starting to see the economics of offshore wind stabilize before what I expect will be a cost out again.

insights.claim: The 2020-2025 downturn saw many failed tenders where wind farms were won but never built, driven by inflation, interest rates, and European tender frameworks becoming an experimental test lab.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Points to policy design risk in European auctions; watch which tender structures actually produce built capacity versus paper awards.

insights.claim: Ørsted distinguishes its US business, where the writedowns occurred, from its European offshore wind business, which it continued to deliver on through the pricing spikes.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: The company frames US losses as geographically contained; investors should separate US impairment noise from the underlying European operating performance.

insights.claim: One gigawatt of offshore wind represents 30-40 billion Danish kroner of capital allocation, underscoring the extreme capital intensity behind headline gigawatt targets.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Reframes gigawatt announcements as multi-billion capex commitments; a lens for assessing balance sheet capacity of any developer chasing large pipelines.
insights.quote: One gawatt of offshore wind is is 30 40 billion Danish corner in terms of sort of capital allocation.

themes.theme: Capital Raise, Ownership and Risk Discipline

insights.claim: Ørsted's 8 billion euro equity raise, announced August 11 2025, is the biggest capital raise ever done for renewables and the biggest ever in the Nordics, with the Danish state contributing about 4 billion euros.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Scale of the raise signals both the depth of Ørsted's balance sheet stress and heavy state backing; dilution and sovereign dependence are key factors for equity holders.
insights.quote: 8 billion euros of equity. Biggest capital race ever done for renewables. Biggest capital race ever done in the Nordics.

insights.claim: Ørsted is roughly six quarters into a three-year turnaround plan and describes itself as on track with firm ground under its feet.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: A mid-turnaround checkpoint; measure future results against the three-year plan timeline to judge whether the recovery narrative holds.

insights.claim: Ørsted's CEO openly acknowledges a real risk of becoming too risk-averse after the raise, citing not winning the latest Danish tender, but frames caution as accountability to investors.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals Ørsted may cede some near-term growth/tenders to protect commitments; a trade-off between pipeline growth and balance sheet safety worth tracking.
insights.quote: Yes, there is a risk because for me it is incredibly important that we deliver on the commitments to all of the investors that I looked in the eye

insights.claim: Ørsted is 50% owned by the Danish state with two other large shareholders plus over 200,000 retail investors, and Equinor holds roughly 10%.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Ownership structure shapes governance and risk appetite; the Equinor stake is the backdrop to recurring merger speculation.

insights.claim: Ørsted's CEO declined to entertain a merger of activities with Equinor, saying focus is on the existing turnaround plan despite prior merger talks.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Merger optionality with Equinor exists but is not being pursued now; a potential future catalyst if the turnaround stalls.

insights.claim: Ørsted announced early and publicly it would reduce headcount by around 25%, to be finalized by the back end of next year.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: A 25% workforce cut quantifies the cost restructuring underpinning the turnaround margin story.
insights.quote: reduce the number of people in with around 25%. even though we will only be finalized by that by the back end of next year

insights.claim: European electricity demand is likely to nearly double by 2050 relative to today, driven substantially by electrification and AI, which needs electrons not molecules.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: A doubling of power demand underpins the long-run bull case for all generation; positions offshore wind and grid buildout as structural growth even amid near-term wobbles.
insights.quote: AI doesn't need molecule. It it needs needs electrons.

insights.claim: Europe imports close to 400 billion euros of fossil fuels, and geopolitical shocks including events in Iran have reframed renewables as a matter of energy security and affordability, not just climate.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: The investment driver has shifted from climate policy to security and cost; renewables demand becomes more resilient to political swings on climate.
insights.quote: you import close to 400 billion euros of fossil fuels is simply not uh sustainable

insights.claim: Nine European states committed in Hamburg to tendering up to 300 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2050, with unusual clarity on the how, not just the target.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete 300 GW ambition with implementation detail; the key watch item is whether governments deliver on stated intentions, which the CEO calls the binding constraint.
insights.quote: committed to tendering out up to 300 gawatt of offshore wind by 2050

insights.claim: The cheapest whole-system energy solution for Europe over coming decades is largely renewables-based, but requires the full stack of solar, onshore wind, batteries, offshore wind and peak gas rather than any single source.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Frames solar vs wind as complementary not either/or; supports diversified exposure across the renewables and storage stack plus flexible gas.
insights.quote: it's not either or you you need it all.

insights.claim: Ørsted's data across nearly 40 years of turbine sensor readings shows no trend of declining wind, and 2025 is actually above the norm for wind, contradicting perceptions of less wind in Europe.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Counters a bear thesis about structurally declining wind resource; supports long-term generation assumptions in offshore wind valuations.
insights.quote: we don't see a trend where it's it's blowing less. It might feel so.

themes.theme: Strategy, Technology Choices and Competitive Moat

insights.claim: Ørsted deliberately narrowed strategy to bottom-fixed offshore wind only, stepping away from floating wind and green fuels and selling its European onshore business.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: A focused pure-play bet on bottom-fixed offshore; simplifies the investment thesis and signals exit from lower-conviction adjacencies.
insights.quote: we stepped away from floating, we stepped away from green fuels, we sold our Europe onshore business.

insights.claim: Ørsted's CEO expects floating offshore wind to take longer to become viable than the market anticipates because its LCOE remains significantly higher than bottom-fixed, only justified where no other options exist.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: A bearish near-term timing call on floating wind from the sector leader; tempers expectations for floating-focused developers and suppliers.
insights.quote: the LCE of floating is simply significantly higher than it is for bottom fix.

insights.claim: Ørsted operates over 1,500 turbines and 18 gigawatts of offshore wind, positioning fleet scale and construction risk-mitigation capability as its core competitive moat outside China.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Quantifies Ørsted's operating scale as a durable advantage; scale-driven cost and operational data are the moat to watch versus new entrants.
insights.quote: we have 18 gawatt of offshore wind. We have more than 1500 turbines spinning.

insights.claim: Ørsted's largest wind farm Hornsea covers an area 135 times Central Park with turbines over 200m tall, and the next phase (Hornsea 3) uses turbines close to 300m tall.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Rising turbine size drives energy yield per unit and is a key lever in the coming cost-out; a metric for tracking technology-led cost declines.
insights.quote: One turbine is more than 200 m tall. One one turbine rotation will power a family for 24 hours.

themes.theme: China and the Global Supply Chain

insights.claim: Ørsted is deliberately not active in China as a developer or as a sourcing OEM base, positioning itself as the global offshore wind leader outside China.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Defines Ørsted's addressable market as ex-China; relevant for sizing growth against China's rapid domestic offshore buildout.

insights.claim: Offshore wind is a globally integrated supply chain in which the industry sources monopiles, cables and vessels from China even while European turbines dominate outside China.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Highlights component-level China dependence beneath a European turbine narrative; a supply-chain and tariff exposure to monitor.
insights.quote: the industry is getting monopiles uh from China... the industry is getting cables from China. The industry is getting vessels from China

insights.claim: The European offshore wind supply chain has invested 14 billion euros over the last three years in factories, ports and vessels, which Ørsted argues is enough to deliver the planned buildout.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals European supply capacity is scaling; reduces the bottleneck bear case and supports feasibility of the 300 GW ambition.
insights.quote: the European supply chain as a whole has invested 14 billion euros in manufacturing capacity

insights.claim: Chinese turbines are currently not part of the eligible mix under European frameworks, and are absent from Ørsted's active markets in Europe, Taiwan, Korea, Australia and the US.
insights.speaker: Rasmus Errboe (Ørsted CEO)
insights.so_what: Regulatory exclusion protects Western turbine makers in these markets; a policy moat whose durability affects Vestas/Siemens Gamesa-type suppliers.
insights.quote: Chinese turbines is not part of the mix.
